newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Hyundai Motor takes on the Japanese.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Hyundai Motor takes on the Japanese.

text.p: Hyundai Motor Co Ltd's $6 billion investment plan to become a top-10 global player is a gamble likely to pay off, analysts said on Friday.
The country's Number One car maker announced this week it would pour billions of dollars into developing its own technology, breaking its reliance on Japanese know-how.
Hyundai now produces mainly small, lower-end cars, but by spending five trillion won ($6.0 billion) until 2000 it aims to develop a range of mid-sized models to compete with Japanese rivals.
"Hyundai now has an economy of size and is ready for global competition," said Jon Chong-hwa, an analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities. "But its product mix is inclined towards low-end products."

Like other South Korean car makers, Hyundai is being driven overseas by an overcrowded domestic market. Sluggish sales at home are eating into already-thin profit margins from production of relatively cheap cars.
South Korea's car production capacity last year was 3.5 million against domestic sales of 1.5 million.
"The move is a means of survival," said Kang Hun-sok, automobile analyst at ING-Barings Securities. "This is a good strategy Hyundai took to expand internationally."
Hyundai Motor, the flagship of the Hyundai Group HYGR.CN, has targeted annual production capacity of 2.4 million cars by 2000 against a forecast 1.43 million this year.
"Hyundai Motor needs to secure the right research and development capability that would go hand-in-hand with production capacity," a company statement said.
For years, South Korea's car industry has focused on size and neglected research and development, analysts say.
Hyundai has leaned on Mitsubishi technology.
"Now they'll try to rely entirely on in-house technology," said Kang. "Hyundai's focus will be mid-size, upper-scale models because of good margins."
"Hyundai's weakness in engine technology will force the car maker to put a lot of focus on engine development," said Jon of Hannuri-Salomon.

By 1998, Hyundai plans to build electric-powered cars and vehicles that run on liquefied natural gas. It will also try to shorten the development time for new models to an average 24 months from 34 months, cutting costs and satisfying fast-changing consumer tastes.
To achieve all this it plans to hire 3,600 more researchers, giving it an army of 10,000 by the end of the century.
"The investment will pay off gradually starting in 2000," said Jon. "It will enable Hyundai to produce cheap but high quality cars that can compete against its Japanese rivals."
Company spokesman Park Chan-keun said the bulk of investment would go towards developing new car models. "It costs about 500 billion won to introduce one new model," he said.

Hyundai plans to invest 640 billion won in research and development this year -- 5.3 percent of expected turnover. It will gradually increase spending to 14.5 trillion won in 2000, or eight percent of expected sales. ($1 = 829 won)
